title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractAdeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455–457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100–1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

MainT cells are at the forefront of cancer immunotherapy1,2,3,4,5,6,7. The US Food and Drug Administration has approved seven chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell products for treating hematological malignancies, including B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL)8,9, large B cell lymphoma10,11,12,13, mantle-cell lymphoma14, follicular lymphoma15 and multiple myeloma16,17, as well as the first T cell receptor (TCR) T cell therapy product, Tecelra (afamitresgene autoleucel), for treating a solid tumor, metastatic synovial sarcoma. Numerous clinical trials to treat solid tumors underway7,18,19. Several approaches have been used to produce human CAR-T cells and other cell-based immunotherapies20,21. The most widely used gene delivery systems are lentiviruses or gammaretroviruses, which are the basis for all currently approved CAR-T products. However, these vectors integrate semirandomly, which can lead to transgene silencing22 and clustering of integration near transcriptional start sites23,24, posing a risk of insertional mutagenesis and oncogenic transformation25,26,27,28,29,30. Safety considerations motivate the development of gene delivery strategies that provide improved control over transgene expression and enhanced targeting specificity.AAV-based vectors may provide an attractive alternative because of their favorable safety profile and compatibility with precise genome engineering. Targeted transgene integration in primary human T cells has been successfully achieved through the use of AAV and CRISPR technologies31,32. However, there is a need for AAV serotypes that enable more efficient transduction of human T cells. AAV6 has shown acceptable delivery efficiency only at very high doses, with multiplicity of infection (MOI) ranging from 1 × 105 to 1 × 106 viral genomes (vg) per cell31,33,34. Such high MOI can result in toxicity to T cells, trigger immune responses35,36 and increase the cost and potential off-target effects37.Here, we evolved AAV capsids directly in primary human T cells and identified a family of variants carrying an APR motif in variable region IV (VR-IV), among which AAV.APR31 (also termed HONG31) emerged as a lead candidate with markedly enhanced tropism for human T and NK cells. Mechanistic studies revealed that AAV.APR31 exploits a CD7-dependent entry route while retaining the canonical AAVR pathway, defining a layered-entry mechanism that accounts for its potent yet lineage-restricted lymphoid transduction. Functionally, a single capsid AAV.APR31 supports transient transgene expression, CRISPR-mediated targeted knock-in and AAV-Sleeping Beauty (SB) transposon delivery, thereby enabling CAR-T, TCR-T and CAR-NK cell engineering ex vivo, as well as direct in vivo CAR-T cell generation in both hematologic and solid tumor models. Under matched conditions in primary human T cells, AAV.APR31 further outperformed the concurrently reported human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7 (ref. 38). Together, these findings show that AAV.APR31 is an evolved lymphotropic AAV capsid that, unlike existing single-modality delivery systems, enables transient and stable engineering across T and NK cells.ResultsDirected evolution identifies a family of APR-motif-enriched AAV capsid variants with human T cell tropismWe engineered an AAV capsid library using AAV6 as a starting serotype, given its prior use in human T cell gene-editing applications31,34,39. We performed saturation mutagenesis on a pseudotyped AAV2/6 genome, comprising the AAV2 Rep region and the AAV6 Cap region flanked by AAV2 inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) (Fig. 1a). We targeted VR-IV of the VP1 capsid protein (amino acids 454–460), a known surface-exposed domain involved in host interaction and antibody neutralization40. For functional selection, we screened the library directly in primary human T cells. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy donors were activated using human CD3/CD28/CD2 T cell activator and transduced with the AAV capsid library at MOI = 1,000 (MOI = 500 for the third round of selection), that is, 1,000 vg per cell. To enrich for capsid variants capable of successful cellular entry, cells were subjected to stringent washes to remove surface-bound and unbound viruses. Internalized viral DNA was extracted; then, the VR-IV region was amplified by PCR and subsequently recloned into the AAV6-based plasmid backbone (the wild-type VR-IV DNA sequence was replaced with EGFP to avoid any capsid6 contamination during the library cloning) to generate a new capsid library for the next round of selection (Fig. 1a). Even among the top 1,000 variants from both donor screens, the APR-containing capsids demonstrated substantially higher enrichment compared to the non-APR counterparts (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).AAV.APR31 enables efficient transgene delivery in human and mouse T and NK cellsTo determine whether APR-containing AAV variants outperform AAV6 in T cell transduction, we focused on AAV.APR31, one of the most enriched variants. First, we assessed its AAV packaging yield by producing a self-complementary AAV (scAAV) vector carrying an EGFP cassette (scAAV-CAG-EGFP) and a single-stranded AAV (ssAAV) vector carrying a CD22-CAR cassette (Fig. 2a). AAV.APR31 yielded 1.02 × 1014 vg per L and 1.63 × 1013 vg per L of medium for EGFP and CD22-CAR cassette packaging, respectively, compared to 2.29 × 1014 vg per L and 2.87 × 1013 vg per L for parental AAV6 under matched production conditions (Fig. 2b). We packaged scAAV-CAG-EGFP either with AAV.APR31 or AAV6 and then transduced Jurkat at MOIs ranging from 50 to 1,000; EGFP expression was measured by flow cytometry 48 h later (Fig. 2e). Notably, AAV.APR31 achieved 26.47% EGFP-positive cells at an MOI of 100 versus 0.84% for AAV6, increased to 58.07% versus 5.07% at an MOI of 250 and exceeded 90% at an MOI of 1,000 versus 18.13% for AAV6 (Fig. 2f,g). To independently validate these findings at the transcript level, we quantified EGFP mRNA by reverse transcription (RT)–qPCR in the same experimental conditions. Consistent with the flow cytometry data, EGFP transcript levels were markedly higher in AAV.APR31-transduced Jurkat cells compared to AAV6 across all MOIs tested (Extended Data Fig. 2a), confirming that the superior transduction efficiency of AAV.APR31 is reflected at both mRNA and protein levels. Lastly, we evaluated primary T cells from multiple donors (Fig. 2h). Even at a relatively low MOI of 250, AAV.APR31 outperformed AAV6 transduced at a much higher MOI of 10,000 (donor 300F: 16.7% versus 13.1%, respectively; donor E: 17.2% versus 15.0%, respectively) on day 5 after donor human T cell activation (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). To assess the applicability of AAV.APR31 across diverse genetic backgrounds and at different stages of T cell activation, we repeated the transduction experiments using primary human T cells from 11 additional donors. Four donors were transduced at an early time point (day 2), whereas seven donors were transduced at a later time point after T cell activation (day 5) (Fig. 2k–m). Consistently, AAV.APR31 exhibited robust transduction efficiency across all samples. We also evaluated the ability of AAV.APR31 to transduce mouse CD8+ T and NK cells using an EGFP reporter. AAV.APR31 demonstrated markedly higher transduction efficiency compared to parental AAV6 in both cell types (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e).AAV.APR31-mediated potent site-specific transgene knock-in in human T cellsTo assess the dependence on dosing, we targeted the first exon of the TRAC locus (a gene encoding the TCR alpha chain) to create universal allogeneic T cells31,41,42 (Fig. 3a), which eliminates endogenous TCR signaling interference43. Given that our approach targets a single genomic locus, the theoretical maximum integration is two copies per cell (one per allele). We observed that the mean CAR copy number in AAV.APR31-transduced cells was comparable to that of AAV6-transduced cells (1.34 versus 1.69 copies per cell; Extended Data Fig. 2j) and neither group exceeded the expected diploid maximum of two copies per cell. These findings indicate that the superior knock-in efficiency of AAV.APR31, reflected by a higher frequency of CAR+ cells, is driven by an increased proportion of successfully edited cells rather than by supraphysiological multicopy integration events. Therefore, we assessed whether AAV.APR31 could support knock-in in bulk CD8+ T cells that were not deliberately prestimulated ex vivo (Fig. 3b). Because HDR is restricted to cycling cells, we characterized the activation state of the cells before editing. Compared to antibody-activated T cells (day 2: 91.9% CD69+, 95.0% CD25+; day 4: 41.3% CD69+, 94.5% CD25+), nonprestimulated cells showed only partial activation (40.3% CD69+, 5.7% CD25+) (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l) while retaining a partially detectable Ki67+ fraction (Extended Data Fig. 2m). Under these conditions, AAV.APR31 mediated efficient knock-in that markedly exceeded AAV6 (13% versus 1.99% at MOI = 100; 35.8% versus 2.95% at MOI = 1,000) (Fig. 3f). In the Jurkat screen, genes such as CD7, TM9SF2, KIAA0319L, VPS52, VPS51, VPS16, ATP2C1, TRAPPC1, GPR108, KPNA6, NR4A1, HELQ, KMT2D, SASH3, COG4, OSBPL8 and SLC35B2 were strongly enriched (Fig. 4c,d and Supplementary Table 2). Viral vectors such as gammaretrovirus and lentivirus pose limitations including semirandom genomic integration, whereas nonviral methods, such as mRNA, HDR DNA templates and transposon systems, offer improved safety but are often limited by low efficiency, transient expression and cellular toxicity.
